messages.author: 9783d9fe56013431
messages.subject: Re: Used ggplot2 in a scientific publication?
parts:
I want to use ggplot2 figures in publications and could really use
some pointers regarding this. Has anyone played around with data dense
figures and how to get them to be manageable in size, appropriate in
font, easy to put into Word or Powerpoint documents and still good
quality? My dataset is very large (25,000 rows) so each plot has
thousands of points that went into its creation.

I'm finding that the pdfs I write to (using code below) are gigantic
and cause Word, Powerpoint, and Preview to struggle. For example, when
I open a PDF using Preview, each layer of each figure is built slowly
and painfully, taking more than 30 seconds even though the pdf might
only be a few pages long.

As an example, I've been using the following commands:


pdf(file="TEST.pdf", width=12, height=8)
pushViewport(viewport(layout = grid.layout(2, 1)))

a<-ggplot(data=subset(all, (Arm=="2R") &(x.m.cov >25000)&(x.s.cov
>25000)) , aes(block)) +
geom_rect(aes(xmin=0 ,xmax=60000000, ymin= 0, ymax=max(ms.x.shared) ),
fill="white")+
geom_rect(aes(xmin=18930000,xmax=26764357, ymin= 0, ymax=max
(ms.x.shared) ), fill="grey80")+
geom_rect(aes(xmin=26784357,xmax=31450000, ymin= 0, ymax=max
(ms.x.shared) ), fill="grey90")+
geom_line(aes(y = ms.x.shared, colour = "Shared polymorphisms
between M and S "), size= .75) +
geom_line(aes(y = ms.x.fixed, colour = "Fixed differences between M
and S "), size= .75) +
labs(x = "2R (in Mb)", y = "Proportion of sites") + opts
(axis.title.x=theme_text(size=12), axis.title.y=theme_text
(size=12,angle = 90)) +
opts(title = "Polymorphisms and fixed differences in 50kb windows,
minimum coverage per window=25kb") + opts(plot.title = theme_text
(size=12)) +
scale_colour_discrete("Site type") +
scale_x_continuous(breaks=c
(0,10000000,20000000,30000000,40000000,50000000,60000000), labels=c
("0 TELOMERIC", "10 ", "20 ","30 ", "40 ", "50 ",
"60 CENTROMERIC")) +
scale_colour_brewer(palette="Dark2") +
opts(axis.text.x = theme_text(colour = "black", vjust=1))+
opts(axis.text.y = theme_text(colour = "black", hjust=1)) +
theme_bw()

b<- more of the same


print(a, vp = viewport(layout.pos.row = 1, layout.pos.col = 1))
print(b, vp = viewport(layout.pos.row = 2, layout.pos.col = 1))

dev.off()

I've played around with pointsize and I've played around with
"reducing file size" after the pdf is created using preview but none
of this seems to help.

Does anyone have tips on producing figures for publication quality
that are not gigantic? All suggestions welcome. Thank you.

messages.author: 5a1b5a9591c118ef
messages.subject: Re: Used ggplot2 in a scientific publication?
parts:
It's hard to tell without your data. I think there is a section on
this in the ggplot2 book with some general advice for publication. I'd
suggest one of the two,

1) sample the data down to a reasonable number of points (who can read
millions of points on print anyway?)

2) use the png device with high enough resolution.

baptiste

> You don't say what sort of plot you are making, but, e.g. a scatterplot with
> thousands of dots isn't going to be very useful, regardless of device - even if
> you make the dots nearly transparent.

A plot like the one produced by smoothScatter (try
example(smoothScatter)) could work very well, though. For ggplot2, the
closest thing is probably the ‘hex’ geom. (But hexbinplot in the
‘hexbin’ package is more advanced, and has more and better-looking
options than the ggplot2 implementation, IMHO.)

--

messages.author: fc22cb727156ff4f
messages.subject: Re: Used ggplot2 in a scientific publication?
parts: On 2009-May-13  , at 07:20 , squid wrote:

> I'm finding that the pdfs I write to (using code below) are gigantic
> and cause Word, Powerpoint, and Preview to struggle. For example, when
> I open a PDF using Preview, each layer of each figure is built slowly
> and painfully, taking more than 30 seconds even though the pdf might
> only be a few pages long.

The journal you are submitting to probably has some requirements in
terms of figure formats (such as EPS or TIFF 1200 dpi for line art,
TIFF 600 dpi for pictures, which are insane but classic ones). Given
your issues, you could indeed go the raster route, but R cannot
produce TIFF so just output PNG at the appropriate resolution and then
convert it to TIFF <rant>why, oh why are publishers still requiring
TIFF when PNG is a lossless compression and does not have the cross
platform issue TIFF has in the order of channels?</rant>
However, as others have mentioned, the issue might be with the type of
plot you are trying to produce rather than with the file format. I
would use geom_density2d with fill=..density.. instead of a scatter
plot with that many points.

JiHO

messages.author: 6d1cd0a71e6148df

parts: hadley wickham skreiv:

> I guess it's just a difference of aesthetic opinion - I think those
> examples are ugly!
>
> I do need to figure out how to make it possible to scale the size of
> the hexes though.
>

Yes, that would be useful. I like the style="lattice" in hexbin

plot(hexbin(x,y),style="lattice")

and it’s possible to achieve something similar with

qplot(x,y,data=d,stat="binhex",geom="point",size=..count..)

but of course that’s not hexagons.

BTW, didn’t the old ggplot (not ggplot2) package have quite a different
hexbin implementation?

--
Karl Ove Hufthammer
